care: The City of God is a work of Christian theology and of argument against the Roman religion of its day. The lesson presents Augustine’s beliefs and arguments as his own, and notes where readers have disagreed. It mentions the sack of Rome and other wars without detail.

young.html: In AD 410 an army of Goths broke into the city of Rome and looted it for three days. Rome had not been captured by an enemy in 800 years. People all over the empire were shocked. Some said: this happened because Rome stopped worshiping the old gods and became Christian.

Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, wrote a huge book to answer them. He called it the City of God. He said that there are really two “cities” in the world, two kinds of people mixed together everywhere. They are not two places on a map. One is made of people who love themselves most of all. The other is made of people who love God most of all, and their neighbors as themselves. Augustine believed that earthly cities, even Rome, rise and fall, but that the city of God would last forever.

young.name: gb-two-cities
young.cap: Augustine’s two cities, running side by side through the ages of history. Tap an age.

young.html: Two kinds of towns. Draw two small towns side by side. In the first, everyone does whatever is best for themselves. In the second, everyone thinks first of others. Draw what the playground, the shops and the roads look like in each. Then talk: which town would you want to live in? Which one is more like the real world, or is ours a mix, as Augustine thought?

full.html: Augustine (AD 354–430) had been bishop of Hippo, in North Africa, for about fifteen years when the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome in August 410. Refugees reached Africa with their stories, and with a charge: Rome’s gods had protected it for a thousand years, and now that the empire had turned to Christianity they had abandoned it. Encouraged by his friend Marcellinus, an imperial official sent to Africa, Augustine began the City of God in 413 and finished it in 426, four years before he died.

full.text: The glorious city of God is my theme in this work, which you, my dearest son Marcellinus, suggested, and which is due to you by my promise. I have undertaken its defence against those who prefer their own gods to the Founder of this city. … A great work this, and an arduous; but God is my helper.

full.work: The City of God, Book I, preface

head: Books
What Augustine argues
rows: The old gods did not give Rome its earthly success, and disasters struck Rome long before Christianity.
Nor can they give happiness after death. Here he engages the best pagan thinkers, especially the Platonists, with respect and with disagreement.
The beginnings of the two cities: creation, the angels, the first human beings.
Their course through history, from Cain and Abel to his own time.
Their ends: peace, judgment, and the eternal city.

full.text: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self. The former, in a word, glories in itself, the latter in the Lord.
full.author: Augustine
full.work: The City of God, Book XIV, chapter 28
full.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

full.html: The two cities are defined by what people love most, not by where they live. In this life they are mixed together: the city of God is a pilgrim, a traveler passing through, living among the earthly city and using its peace. Augustine does not simply equal one city with the Church and the other with the Roman state; he says the true membership of each will be known only at the end.

full.html: One of Augustine’s sharpest pages asks what makes a government different from a gang.

full.text: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms? … Indeed, that was an apt and true reply which was given to Alexander the Great by a pirate who had been seized. For when that king had asked the man what he meant by keeping hostile possession of the sea, he answered with bold pride, “What thou meanest by seizing the whole earth; but because I do it with a petty ship, I am called a robber, whilst thou who dost it with a great fleet art styled emperor.”
full.author: Augustine
full.work: The City of God, Book IV, chapter 4
full.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

full.html: The pirate story was older; Augustine found it in Cicero. His point is that size and success do not make a state just. What makes a government more than a band of robbers is justice.

In Book XIX Augustine argues that everyone, even people at war, wants peace of some kind, and defines it in a phrase that became famous: peace is “the tranquillity of order” (tranquillitas ordinis), each thing in its proper place. Earthly peace is good and both cities use it, he says, but it is always partial and fragile. Only the city of God, in his belief, will know perfect peace.

Reading the book as a plan for a Christian government. Augustine is not drawing up a constitution. He is arguing that no earthly state, Christian or not, should be mistaken for the city of God, and that Christians should be good citizens of the earthly city while not putting their final hope in it. Later readers have drawn very different political conclusions from the book.

items: A philosophy of history: Augustine read all of history as one story with a direction and an end, instead of endless cycles. That idea shaped Western thinking about history for centuries.

Church and state: medieval writers argued over his two cities when they debated the powers of popes and kings. His biographer Einhard says Charlemagne liked to have the City of God read to him at dinner.
Politics without illusions: modern thinkers of many kinds still cite his view that states are needed to keep a limited peace, but are never perfect.

deep.text: Context: the end of an age

deep.html: The Western Roman Empire was weakening. Augustine died in 430 while the Vandals were besieging his own city of Hippo. Some later readers have seen the City of God as the farewell of the ancient world and the first great book of the Middle Ages. It argues with Roman history, Varro’s writings on the gods, Cicero’s Republic and the Platonists, and so preserves much of what they said.

items: What do you love most? Augustine thought that answer shows which “city” a person belongs to. Is he right that what we love shapes who we are?
What makes a government different from a gang of robbers?
Can a country be good if it does not last? Can it be great if it is not just?
Is peace just the absence of war, or something more?

deep.html: Thomas Aquinas, in the next era, drew on Augustine while giving more room to natural reason in political life. Dante pictured the eternal city in his Paradiso. Machiavelli, later on this ladder, asked what rulers must do to keep a state in a world where people are not good, a very different starting point. Gibbon, in the 18th century, blamed Christianity in part for Rome’s fall, reviving the very charge Augustine answered; historians since have weighed many other causes.

questions: Augustine says two cities are made by two loves: love of self and love of God. What would a town look like if everyone in it loved others as themselves?
What is the difference between a king and a pirate, according to the pirate? Do you agree?
Why might people look for someone to blame after a disaster? Is that fair?
Augustine called peace “the tranquillity of order.” What would that mean in your home or classroom?
Can something be great without being good?
